## Regression Scenario {.unnumbered}

A professor studies the relationship between weekly study time and exam score.

- $Y$ = exam score from 0 to 100
- $X$ = hours studied during the week before the exam

The fitted regression is

$$
\widehat{\text{Score}} = 58.4 + 3.15(\text{Study Hours}).
$$

The 95% confidence interval for the slope is

$$
(1.91,\;4.39).
$$

For a student who studies 6 hours:

- fitted mean score = **77.3**
- 95% confidence interval for the **mean score** = **(74.9, 79.7)**
- 95% prediction interval for **one new student's score** = **(66.2, 88.4)**

Observed study times range from **1 to 10 hours**.

## Which interpretation would you defend?

Consider these interpretations of the slope 3.15.

**A.** "If a student studies one additional hour, their exam score will increase by 3.15 points."

**B.** "Students who study one additional hour tend to score about 3.15 points higher on average."

**C.** "For every one-hour difference in study time, the model predicts a 3.15-point difference in the mean exam score."

Circle one choice for each statement.

| Statement | Accept | Revise | Reject |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | ○ | ○ | ○ |
| B | ○ | ○ | ○ |
| C | ○ | ○ | ○ |

**Briefly explain your choices.**

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution"}
| Statement | Assessment | Reason |
|:--:|:--|:--|
| **A** | **Reject as stated** | This asserts a guaranteed **individual change** and a **causal effect**. Neither follows from the fitted observational regression. |
| **B** | **Accept with a clarification** | It communicates an **association in average exam scores**, not a guaranteed increase for a particular student. Better wording: "Students who study one hour more tend to have exam scores about 3.15 points higher, on average." |
| **C** | **Accept** | This is the most precise interpretation: it explicitly refers to a difference in the **predicted conditional mean**. |

For two study times $x$ and $x+1$,

$$
\widehat{E}(Y\mid X=x+1)-\widehat{E}(Y\mid X=x)
=3.15.
$$

The model describes differences in conditional means; it does not prove that an intervention increasing an individual's study time by one hour would raise their score by 3.15 points.

**Additional inference:** The slope's 95% confidence interval, $(1.91,4.39)$, excludes zero. Under the usual regression assumptions, this provides evidence of a positive association, but still does not establish causation.
:::

## What would you tell this student?

A student says:

> "I plan to study 6 hours. The regression says my score should be between 74.9 and 79.7."

What would you change or clarify?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution"}
The interval **(74.9, 79.7)** is a 95% **confidence interval for the population mean exam score among students studying 6 hours**, not an interval intended to cover an individual student's score.

The fitted mean is **77.3**. Individual scores vary around that mean, so a substantially wider interval is appropriate for predicting one student's outcome.

<!-- A better statement is: "The estimated average score for students who study 6 hours is 77.3, and the 95% confidence interval for that mean is (74.9, 79.7)." -->

The interval **(74.9, 79.7)** is a confidence interval for the **mean score** among students who study 6 hours.

To predict the score of **one new student**, report the fitted score and its **prediction interval**:

$$
\widehat{Y}(6)=58.4+3.15(6)=\boxed{77.3},
$$

$$
\boxed{\text{95\% prediction interval: }(66.2,\;88.4).}
$$

The prediction interval is wider because it accounts for both uncertainty about the mean response and the variation of **individual scores** around that mean. The 95% refers to the long-run coverage of the prediction-interval procedure under the model assumptions; it does **not** guarantee that this particular student's score will fall within the interval.

:::

Now suppose another student plans to study **15 hours**. The fitted value is

$$
58.4 + 3.15(15) = 105.65.
$$

Would you trust this prediction? Why or why not?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution"}
**No.** The observed study times were only **1 to 10 hours**. A prediction at 15 hours is **extrapolation**, which assumes that the fitted linear relationship continues beyond the observed data without supporting evidence.

In addition, **105.65 exceeds the exam's maximum possible score of 100**. This is a clear warning that the simple linear model is unsuitable for this extrapolation. We should not interpret 105.65 as a plausible literal exam score.
:::

**(MSSC)** Suppose we redefine the predictor as

$$
X_c = X - 5,
$$

so that $X_c=0$ corresponds to studying 5 hours. Without refitting the model, determine the new regression equation. What changes about the intercept and slope? Would any fitted values or predictions change? Explain.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution (MSSC)"}
Since $X=X_c+5$, substitute into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{Y}
&=58.4+3.15X\\
&=58.4+3.15(X_c+5)\\
&=(58.4+15.75)+3.15X_c\\
&=\boxed{74.15+3.15X_c}.
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Intercept:** Changes from **58.4** (predicted score at 0 study hours) to **74.15** (predicted score at 5 study hours).
- **Slope:** Remains **3.15 points per study hour**, because subtracting a constant from $X$ does not change the unit or scale of a one-hour difference.
- **Fitted values and predictions:** **Unchanged**, because the new equation represents exactly the same fitted line in a different coordinate system. Residuals and model fit are also unchanged.

For example, 6 study hours means $X_c=1$:

$$
\widehat Y=74.15+3.15(1)=77.3.
$$

The standard error and confidence interval of the **intercept** can change, because the intercept now represents the mean at a different study time. The slope estimate and its confidence interval do not change under this recentering.
:::
